To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have shown for the first time the existence of a transition from fractional to classical diffusion in the Stokes–Einstein equation for a simple fluid and have determined the particle size and concentration dependence of this transition for the first time.

we have used optical microscopy to track the motion of individual particles in simple fluids and found that there is a transition in the diffusion behaviour of particles from molecular to particle-like behaviour at diameters of 150–300 nm.

the diffusion of a spherical particle in a liquid is described by the classical (non-fractional) Stokes–Einstein equation for particles larger than a certain diameter that is independent of particle density and viscosity, but dependent on concentration, and that the fractional Stokes– Einstein equation describes diffusion for particles smaller than that diameter.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new optical technique to measure the translational diffusion of single particles.
the development of a new class of optical techniques that are capable of providing a detailed understanding of the dynamics of individual particles suspended in a liquid.
the diffusion of single particles in simple fluids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Stokes–Einstein equation is not applicable for particles with diameters smaller than a certain critical value, which is a function of the concentration and viscosity of the medium.
the Stokes–Einstein relation is valid only for the translational diffusion of spherical molecules in liquids and not for particles.
the Stokes–Einstein relation holds for particles of diameter greater than 300 nm and that the fractional Stokes– Einstein relation holds for particles smaller than 150 nm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fractional Stokes– Einstein behaviour is a molecular phenomenon that applies only to particles with diameters less than 150 nm.
the transition from fractional to classical diffusion occurs in the diameter range of 150–300 nm for a range of concentrations and viscosities.
the transition occurs at particle sizes that depend on the solvent viscosity, the solvent density, and the particle concentration, but are independent of the particle density.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a transition from molecular to particle behaviour in the diffusion of particles in simple fluids.
the transition from molecular to particle behaviour is a real effect that is independent of particle density and is dependent on the concentration and viscosity of the fluid.
the Stokes–Einstein equation can be applied to the motion of single particles in simple fluids provided that the particle is larger than the transition diameter.
